piles.hero.title: Piles (Haemorrhoids) Treatment
piles.hero.lede: Blood, itching or a lump during bowel movements — piles are very common. Treatment is chosen according to the type and severity after an examination.
piles.what.p1: Piles (haemorrhoids, locally called bosa) are swollen veins in and around the anus and in the lowest part of the rectum — similar to varicose veins. They may form inside the anal canal (internal piles), which are usually painless but can bleed, or under the skin around the anus (external piles), which can itch, ache or turn into a tender lump.
piles.what.p2: Piles are very common — many people experience them at some point in life. They are not dangerous in themselves, but their symptoms can overlap with more serious conditions, so new or persistent symptoms should always be assessed by a doctor.
piles.symptoms.i1: Bright red blood after passing stool — on the toilet paper, on the stool surface or in the bowl (often painless)
piles.symptoms.i2: An itchy or irritating feeling around the anus
piles.symptoms.i3: Pain or discomfort around the anus
piles.symptoms.i4: A lump around the anus, which may be tender
piles.symptoms.i5: Mucus on the toilet paper or in the underwear after wiping
piles.symptoms.i6: A feeling of still needing to pass stool after going to the toilet
piles.symptoms.i7: Internal piles can slip down (prolapse) through the anal opening, causing pain and irritation
piles.symptoms.i8: If a clot forms inside an external pile (a thrombosed pile) — severe pain, swelling and a hard, discoloured lump near the anus
piles.causes.p: Piles develop when the veins around the anus stretch under pressure. Things that increase the risk include:
piles.causes.i1: Constipation and straining on the toilet
piles.causes.i2: Sitting for long periods, especially on the toilet
piles.causes.i6: Pregnancy — pressure from the growing baby
piles.causes.i7: Regularly lifting heavy items, and getting older — the supporting tissues weaken and stretch
piles.when.p1: See a doctor for an examination rather than assuming bleeding is just piles — bleeding can have other causes. Especially see a doctor if:
piles.when.i1: there is any bleeding from the back passage, especially the first time it happens
piles.when.i2: symptoms do not improve after about a week of home care, or keep coming back
piles.when.i3: your bowel habit changes, or the colour or consistency of your stool changes
piles.when.i4: there is any noticeable change around the anus that is not normal for you
piles.when.p2: Seek urgent medical care if, alongside piles symptoms, there is a high temperature with shivering, pus leaking from the area, heavy or non-stop bleeding, severe pain, or dizziness and light-headedness — if needed, go to the nearest hospital emergency department.
piles.treat.intro: Treatment depends on the type and severity of the piles — your doctor will examine you and advise what is appropriate for you.
piles.treat.home.d: Keep stools soft with plenty of fibre and fluids; warm baths (sitz baths) can ease itching and pain; an ice pack wrapped in a cloth can ease discomfort; paracetamol can be taken for pain — avoid painkillers containing codeine (they can cause constipation) and avoid ibuprofen if the piles are bleeding. Keep the area clean and dry — pat rather than rub; avoid straining, and do not ignore the urge to pass stool.
piles.treat.med.d: Topical creams, ointments or suppositories to ease pain, itching and swelling; laxatives or stool-softening treatment if constipation is contributing. A pharmacist can suggest suitable products, and a doctor may prescribe stronger treatment if needed.
piles.treat.clinic.d: Rubber band ligation — a small band is placed around the pile so it drops off; sclerotherapy — a solution is injected to shrink the pile; infrared coagulation or electrotherapy — energy is used to cut the blood supply so the pile shrinks. These are usually done with the area numbed, and patients generally go home the same day.
piles.treat.surg.h: Surgery (usually for large or persistent piles)
piles.treat.surg.d: Haemorrhoidectomy — surgical removal of the piles; stapled haemorrhoidopexy — the piles are stapled back inside the anal canal; haemorrhoidal artery ligation — stitches are used to reduce the blood supply so the piles shrink.
piles.treat.out: Which treatment suits you — your doctor will examine you and advise what is appropriate. Piles can come back even after successful treatment.
piles.prevent.i1: Add fibre gradually — fruits, vegetables, whole grains; supplements such as psyllium can help, but drink plenty of water with them
piles.prevent.i2: Drink enough fluids through the day; cutting down alcohol and caffeine may help
piles.prevent.i3: Do not strain, and do not hold your breath on the toilet
piles.prevent.i4: Go as soon as you feel the urge, and do not sit on the toilet longer than needed
piles.prevent.i5: Stay active — exercise helps prevent constipation and reduces pressure on the veins
piles.prevent.i6: Avoid long periods of sitting; take breaks to move around
piles.recov.p: Many people find their symptoms settle with home measures within about a week, though this varies. Office procedures are usually done with the area numbed, and patients generally go home the same day. Surgery may need a short stay or same-day discharge depending on the person and the procedure. Recovery time differs from person to person, and piles can return later — your doctor will advise on follow-up and prevention.
